“We need to change the way we finance election campaigns so candidates can run and win without having to raise big money, and they can spend their time listening to voters rather than their donors,” said Trent Lange, president of California Clean Money Campaign and co-chair of the Yes on Prop. 4 campaign.
Gov. Gavin Newsom (https://calmatters.org/tag/gavin-newsom/) and the Democratic-led state Legislature, which voted last year (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb42) to place Prop. 4 on the November ballot, also support the measure. Sen. Tom Umberg (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/thomas-umberg-165043), a Santa Ana Democrat and a co-author of Prop. 4, said it would help alleviate a “growing cynicism in politics” and allow candidates to spend more time developing policies instead of fundraising.
“To the extent that we can engage particularly small donors, that will … empower and also engage the body politic, particularly young people,” he said.
But opponents say politicians should not use taxpayer dollars (https://caltax.org/prop4/) to run campaigns. They argue the measure would force voters to subsidize candidates they otherwise wouldn’t support, and that fraudulent candidates could exploit the system.
Voters have previously rejected ballot initiatives that would have allowed public money to be used for political campaigns. Nearly two-thirds of voters shot down a 2000 measure that would have allowed candidates to tap public funds for advertising (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2000/25_03_2000.html). In 2010, 58% of voters opposed a 2010 measure (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_15,_Biennial_Lobbyist_Fee_and_Public_Campaign_Funding_Measure_(June_2010)) to lift the 1988 ban.
“The voters have been quite clear they don’t want taxpayer money being used for politics,” Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/carl-demaio-161014), a San Diego Republican, said last year (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/hearings/278290#t=221&f=fe479f37ee7a3df6888379e9be069fd8) on the Assembly floor. “Unfortunately, politicians simply can’t take no for an answer.”

Critics also doubt the effectiveness of Prop. 4, arguing it is not specific enough to have teeth.
Prop. 4 offers only broad instructions to local governments and the state. It would ban candidates from using public funds meant for education, public safety and transportation. It would require candidates to prove they have enough public support and to agree to certain spending limits to receive funding, but doesn’t spell out how much. It would also ban candidates from using the money to pay for legal defenses, fines or personal loans to their campaigns.
The measure specifically exempts the Fair Political Practices Commission, the state’s campaign finance watchdog, from ensuring local programs are not exploited or abused, leaving it largely to local governments. But not every local government has its own watchdog agency, let alone an effective one.
The San Francisco Chronicle’s editorial board, in opposing Prop. 4, argued that its rules “are only meaningful if they’re enforced by independent, nonpartisan bodies. And Prop. 4 offers no guarantee they will be.”
Effectiveness debate
Fifteen states and Washington, D.C., offer some sort of statewide public financing for political campaigns, according to an analysis by the National Conference of State Legislatures (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/public-financing-of-campaigns-overview).
Studies are mixed on the effectiveness of those programs.
Some, including one in 2003 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1532673X03256784) by two University of Maryland scholars, suggest that candidates who accept public financing spend less time fundraising, freeing them up for other campaign activities.
Some researchers found that public financing expanded the pool of candidates running for office. A 2022 study of Seattle’s program (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0047272722000780), which gives each registered voter four $25 vouchers to contribute to the campaign of their choice, concluded that the program boosted the number of candidates by 86%. Another study (https://web.stanford.edu/~neilm/The%20Impact%20of%20Public%20Financing%20on%20Electoral%20Competition.pdf) of Arizona and Maine’s programs found that they “significantly increased competition.”
Others disagreed. The United States Government Accountability Office, the nonpartisan research agency advising Congress, studied Arizona and Maine’s programs (https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-10-390.pdf) in 2010 and concluded there was no evidence that public financing led to more candidates.
There’s little evidence that public financing has curbed the influence of private donors, according to the Seattle study and the GAO report.
In California, few studies have examined the effectiveness of local programs. A 2023 San Francisco Ethics Commission study found candidates have increasingly tapped into the public funds and that third-party spending was “at near all-time lows.” But the commission encouraged a more comprehensive analysis. A 2013 study (https://www.oaklandca.gov/files/assets/city/v/3/boards-amp-commissions/documents/pec/publications/reports-by-third-parties/2013-05-01-evaluating-oaklands-limited-public-financing-act.pdf) in Oakland found no evidence its program diluted the influence of wealthy donors, although it did seem to boost competition.
Researchers point to the difficulty (https://sgp.jhu.edu/primers/public-funding-of-us-elections/#conclusion) of studying public financing programs, because most apply in only a handful of states and it is hard to measure what would have happened if the programs had not been in place.
The lack of compelling evidence makes Prop. 4 proponents’ claims shaky, the San Diego Union-Tribune’s editorial board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/09/04/endorsement-dont-buy-prop-4s-baloney-about-publicly-financed-campaigns/) argued.
“So Proposition 4’s only certain effect would be to create a new category of government spending that taxpayers could be required to pay for — one with no track record of delivering promised benefits,” it said.
The ballot measure should not be overly prescriptive, said Dora Rose, deputy director for the League of Women Voters of California, a co-sponsor of Prop. 4.
“Prop. 4 sets basic safeguards and then lets communities learn from the evidence and decide what works for them,” she said.
For now, voters appear skeptical. A September poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) from the Public Policy Institute of California found 53% of likely voters would oppose Prop. 4, while just 42% would vote yes. Another poll (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf) by the UC-Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies shows a tighter matchup, with 35% of likely voters supporting the measure and another 35% against it.

Should public money fund political campaigns? Taking a look at California’s Prop. 4
By By Kiara Adams, video script produced using AI assistance

Proposition 4 repeals California’s ban on the use of public funds to finance political campaigns. Funds for federal elections would still be banned. Below is a transcript of the video above. Read our voter guide story on Prop. 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html) here, along with the editorial board’s take on the issue (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/election-endorsements/article317448027.html).
Should your tax dollars pay for political campaigns? That’s a question on your California ballot right now.
Here’s the deal with Proposition 4 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317016880.html).
Right now, California bans public money from funding political campaigns, except in a handful of cities like Berkeley and San Francisco. Prop. 4 would change that.
A “yes” vote lets state and local governments create programs that give candidates public funds to run for office, excluding federal races. It wouldn’t require them to. And the money couldn’t come from education, transportation or public safety budgets.
Supporters like the California Clean Money Action Fund say it reduces the power of big-money donors. They say we need to change how campaigns are financed so officials work for people, not wealthy donors.
Opponents, led by the California Taxpayers Association, say tax dollars should go to libraries, roads and schools, not campaign mailers.
A “no” vote keeps the current ban in place.
Your vote decides. Check your ballot and head to sacbee.com (https://www.sacbee.com/) for more on every proposition.

California Voters Will Choose Whether to Allow Public Campaign Financing — Here’s Why It Matters
Public financing is the most effective counter we have to the influence of megadonors in politics.
Celina Avalos Jaramillo (https://www.brennancenter.org/about/staff/celina-avalos-jaramillo)

This November, California voters will decide whether to adopt Proposition 4 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/4/index.htm), a ballot measure that would allow the state to enact public campaign financing programs. Approving the measure would be a powerful way to counter the corrupting influence of big money in state politics. It would allow candidates to run competitive campaigns without depending on large donors and help more Californians engage meaningfully with the political process.
California elections are awash in money. In the 2026 primary elections, outside groups representing some of the state's wealthiest individuals and most powerful business interests spent $9 million (https://www.loscerritosnews.net/2026/05/29/money-floods-ad-67-race-9-million-in-outside-spending-turns-local-assembly-contest-into-proxy-war/) to influence just one assembly district seat. Several billionaires and billionaire-fueled PACs poured (https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jun/01/tech-billionaires-california-elections) millions into other state legislative races that in the past would have been community-focused contests. These developments mirror a larger national trend in which a handful of ultra-wealthy donors increasingly dominate election spending. And this year's midterms are on track (https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/07/extraordinary-amount-money-pouring-into-midterm-elections/) to break spending records, with the top 50 donors (https://www.washingtonpost.com/elections/interactive/2026/06/25/these-are-biggest-individual-donors-2026-election-cycle/) already having poured nearly $1.8 billion into the election. That figure doesn't include an additional reported $276 million (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/12/us/politics/elon-musk-midterms.html) spent by Elon Musk.
Thanks to Citizens United and other court decisions, states and localities cannot limit how much billionaires and wealthy industries like AI, crypto, and hedge funds spend on California elections. But they can provide alternative ways for candidates to reach voters.
One of the most powerful is to provide voluntary public financing for candidates who have demonstrated viability. Public financing programs currently exist (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/guide-public-financing-programs-nationwide) in at least 14 states and 26 localities, including five California charter cities, but state law (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/about-fppc/about-the-political-reform-act/) currently bans other localities and the state from creating similar programs. Prop 4 would repeal that ban, giving the legislature and local governments the opportunity to create new public financing programs.
They would have a number of models to choose from. One of the most effective and best-studied systems is small donor matching, which matches small donations from individuals in the community with public funds. Los Angeles (https://ethics.lacity.gov/publications/matching-funds-faq-2026/), Berkeley (https://berkeleyca.gov/your-government/elections/campaign-finance), Long Beach (https://library.municode.com/ca/long_beach/codes/municipal_code?nodeId=TIT2ADPE_CH2.01THLOBECAREAC), and San Francisco (https://sfethics.org/guidance/campaigns/candidates/public-financing-program) use this model, as do New York State and New York City. Other programs, including statewide systems in Arizona, Connecticut, and Maine, offer qualifying candidates block grants. Another model provides eligible voters with vouchers that they can use to assign public funds to participating candidates, as Oakland (https://www.oaklandca.gov/Government/Boards-Commissions/Public-Ethics-Commission/Democracy-Dollars-Program) will soon do. Prop 4 does not require the state or any locality to adopt any of these systems, or to enact public financing at all. It simply gives them the option.
Some who oppose (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/endorsement-prop-4-public-financing-22426379.php) Prop 4 argue that California's existing public financing programs need further study before expanding the reform in the state. But Prop 4 does not create any new programs - it simply gives the state and localities more options. Jurisdictions across the state that want to implement public financing would still be able to weigh the pros and cons while looking to especially strong models, like New York State, as they develop their own programs.
The benefits of public financing in New York and elsewhere are in fact well-documented. Data from New York State's first cycle (https://pcfb.ny.gov/system/files/documents/2025/01/2024-new-york-state-public-campaign-finance-board-election-cycle-report-final.pdf) of public financing in 2024 shows a remarkable shift (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/new-york-states-public-campaign-financing-program-empowers-constituent) in campaign funding. Publicly financed candidates relied significantly more on small, in-district contributions than in past elections. Roughly twice as many (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/new-york-states-public-campaign-financing-program-empowers-constituent) New Yorkers made small-dollar donations compared to the 2020 or 2022 cycles. The increase in small donations was driven by local constituents, which is striking in a state where out-of-district and out-of-state donors have historically dominated (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/new-york-states-public-campaign-financing-program-empowers-constituent) election giving.
Other jurisdictions have had similar successes. In DC's (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/major-strides-public-campaign-financing) first citywide elections with public financing in 2020, publicly financed candidates tended to outraise and enjoy greater electoral success than their privately financed counterparts. In Seattle, the number of residents donating to city campaigns more than doubled (https://www.seattle.gov/documents/Departments/EthicsElections/DemocracyVoucher/Program%20Data/Reports/2021%20Seattle%20Democracy%20Voucher%20Report.pdf?inline=1) in just the first few years that public financing was available. And after Berkeley, California's public financing program went into effect in 2018, contributions from non-Berkeley residents dropped (https://maplightarchive.org/story/2018-fair-elections-in-berkeley/) to 10 percent of total fundraising that year, down from 33 percent in 2016.

Proposition 4 comes at a critical time, both in California and nationally, when the public is profoundly angry (https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/10/07/extraordinary-amount-money-pouring-into-midterm-elections/) about the impact of wealth in American politics. A majority of Americans (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/05/09/poll-americans-say-too-much-money-in-politics-00912455) across the ideological spectrum say that there is too much money in politics. They're fed up with corruption in government and broadly support (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/poll-voters-want-solutions-government-corruption) major reforms to fix our campaign finance system. It's hardly surprising, then, that a recent poll (https://www.ppic.org/blog/commentary-affordability-is-the-top-issue-on-californias-november-ballot/) of California voters named threats to democracy as the most pertinent issue facing the country.
Americans across the country recognize the problem with the dominance of unchecked wealth in our elections. Proposition 4 presents Californians with an opportunity to shift course and build momentum for more ambitious change nationwide.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.

Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.

Fast Facts
Most electoral campaigns are privately financed. But some states and localities offer programs through which candidates running for state or local offices can use public funds for their campaigns.
We reviewed 5 public financing programs. They all required candidates to collect a specific number of contributions to qualify and then adhere to spending limits.
The average amount of public funding that candidates received varied by office sought. For example, in the 2022 election, mayoral candidates in Los Angeles received about $1.3 million and city council candidates received $198,151.
The average amounts also varied by location.
Skip to Highlights
Highlights
What GAO Found
States and localities have generally implemented public campaign financing programs using one of three models: (1) grants-participating candidates receive lump-sum grants of public funds; (2) matching funds-participating candidates receive public funds matching certain private contributions they raise, at a set rate; and (3) vouchers-eligible residents receive a credit of public funds they can assign to one or more participating candidates. GAO selected five programs representing the three model types (Arizona; Los Angeles, California; Minnesota; Montgomery County, Maryland; and Seattle, Washington) and examined their characteristics. For example, all five programs have requirements for candidates to qualify for the program, and once qualified, to receive public funds. These requirements include, for example, collecting a specific number of contributions to qualify and then adhering to spending limits to receive public funds.
Voting Booths
The amount of public funding participating candidates received varied by office sought and location, among other things. For example, in Minnesota in the 2022 election, legislative candidates received an average of $4,716 in public funds, and the one participating gubernatorial candidate received $584,034 in public funds. In Los Angeles in the 2022 election, participating city council candidates received an average of $198,151 in public funds, and participating mayoral candidates received an average of $1,284,158 in public funds.
GAO interviewed officials from the five selected programs and four additional programs (Albuquerque, New Mexico; Hawaii; Maine; and Washington, D.C.) to obtain perspectives on candidate participation. Officials from all nine programs said that many candidates are attracted to the public campaign financing programs because they provide an accessible source of funding. This may be particularly appealing for candidates with limited fundraising experience. Officials from eight of the nine programs said a key reason candidates may not participate is because they perceive the available public funding to be insufficient to run a competitive campaign.
Why GAO Did This Study
While most electoral campaigns are privately financed, 14 states and 26 localities offer programs through which candidates running for state or local offices can use public funds to finance their campaigns, according to a 2024 Brennan Center for Justice report.
The House committee report accompanying the Financial Services and General Government Appropriations Bill, 2023, includes a provision for GAO to revisit and update its 2010 report ( GAO-10-390 (https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-10-390) ) on public campaign financing programs. This report describes, among other things, (1) key characteristics of public campaign financing programs in selected states and localities; (2) what available data indicate about candidates' use of these programs; and (3) factors affecting candidate participation in these programs.
GAO selected five locations with state and local public campaign financing programs that covered executive and legislative offices, were implemented for at least two election cycles, and represented a mix of program models, among other factors. GAO reviewed relevant laws and documents and interviewed officials to describe key characteristics of the selected programs. GAO also analyzed candidate participation and campaign finance data for these five programs for the two most recent election cycles.
GAO interviewed officials from these five programs and four additional programs-selected using the same criteria-to obtain perspectives on public campaign financing programs. The findings from these interviews are not generalizable, but provide insight into state and local perspectives.
For more information, contact Rebecca Gambler at (202) 512-8777 or gamblerr@gao.gov (mailto:gamblerr@gao.gov).

What is public financing and how does it work?
The vast amounts of money being raised and spent to influence elections has inevitably left many
Americans feeling alienated from the political process. Over $6 billion was spent on federal elections
during the 2016 election cycle alone.1 Despite the election’s exorbitant price tag, only a fraction of
Americans actually gave money to a federal candidate, political party, or PAC in 2016. In fact, just .53% of
the entire U.S. population made a contribution of $200 or more for federal elections in the 2016 cycle.2
Not surprisingly, a 2015 CBS News/N.Y. Times poll found that 66% of Americans believe that the wealthy
have more influence over the election process. Similarly, 46% of Americans supported completely
rebuilding the system for campaign funding, and another 39% felt that “fundamental changes” were
necessary.3
Public financing of elections offers an alternative system of campaign financing that can both expand
participation in the election process and facilitate dialogue between voters and candidates. The idea of
public financing is not new; the first public financing bill was introduced in Congress in 1904. Although
the concept of public financing is by now well-established, these systems remain an innovative approach
to campaign reform intended to broaden democratic participation.
The details of particular public financing programs vary, but all of these systems provide candidates who
choose to participate with public funds to conduct their election campaigns. In exchange for the provision
of public funds, a participating candidate typically agrees to adhere to specific fundraising guidelines such
as lower contribution limits or caps on total campaign spending.
One common public financing structure entails a state or city giving a participating candidate a lump-sum
grant to pay for their entire election campaign. In return, participating candidates agree to run their
campaign with grant funds rather than private contributions. Typically, participating candidates also
agree to a cap on their total campaign spending. These full public funding programs, also known as “Clean

3 https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2015/06/02/us/politics/money-in-politics-poll.html.
Public Financing of Election Campaigns

Elections” programs, are in place in Arizona, Connecticut, Maine, Vermont, and a handful of cities around
the country.
Another popular model of public financing involves a city or state matching each private contribution that
a participating candidate raises with public funds. Like full public funding programs, a candidate who
accepts matching funds typically agrees to limit total campaign spending and other fundraising
requirements inapplicable to non-participating candidates. New York City currently has a matching funds
program available for mayoral and city council candidates, and the city will match each contribution that
a participating candidate receives from a city resident at a six-to-one rate up to $175.4
In 2015, Seattle voters approved a novel system of public financing called the Democracy Voucher
Program.”5 Under Seattle’s program, eligible city residents are provided four $25 vouchers that they can
assign, in any allotment, to participating city candidates of their choice. Participating candidates then
exchange assigned vouchers with the Seattle Ethics and Elections Commission for campaign funds; thus,
assigning a voucher is equivalent to making a political contribution to a candidate. Since the program
does not require Seattle residents to use any personal funds in order to assign a voucher to a candidate,
Democracy Vouchers have the potential to greatly expand political participation among Seattle residents.
What have courts said about public financing?
Since the first public financing programs were enacted in the 1970s, federal courts have consistently
recognized that public funding of election campaigns serves the compelling governmental interest in
preventing actual and apparent political corruption. In the seminal case Buckley v. Valeo, the U.S.
Supreme Court upheld the presidential public financing program as a means “to reduce the deleterious
influence of large contributions on our political process, to facilitate communication by candidates with
the electorate, and to free candidates from the rigors of fundraising.”6 The Court expressly rejected the
contention that public financing violates the First Amendment, explaining that the presidential public
financing program “is a congressional effort, not to abridge, restrict, or censor speech, but rather to use

public money to facilitate and enlarge public discussion and participation in the electoral process, goals
vital to a self-governing people.”7
More recently, the Court affirmed the overall constitutionality of public financing even as it concluded
that “trigger” provisions giving publicly financed candidates additional funds in direct response to
contributions to non-participating opponents and expenditures by outside groups did not pass
constitutional muster.8 In Arizona Free Enterprise, the Court made a point to emphasize that
“governments may engage in public financing of election campaigns and that doing so can further
significant governmental interest [s], such as the state interest in preventing corruption.”9 Thus, Arizona
Free Enterprise did not undercut the constitutionality of voluntary public financing programs generally or
otherwise “call into question the wisdom of public financing as a means of funding political candidacy.” 10
Other federal courts have similarly endorsed public financing as a constitutional means of effectuating
campaign finance reform. Notably, the Second Circuit upheld provisions of New York City’s matching
funds regime imposing special restrictions on contributions from individuals doing business with the
city.11 In its reasoning, the court highlighted that the city’s matching funds system both “encourages small,
individual contributions, and is consistent with [an] interest in discouraging entrenchment of incumbent
candidates.”12
What are the effects of public financing on election
campaigns?
A substantial body of empirical and academic research supports the democratic benefits of public
financing. In particular, research supports that public financing (1) promotes engagement between
candidates and voters, and (2) increases electoral competitiveness.
Public Financing Promotes Engagement
By design, public financing programs encourage candidates to draw more voters into the political process.

In full public financing regimes, an aspiring participant typically must demonstrate viability as a
candidate by raising a certain number of small donations from constituents before becoming eligible for a
grant of public funds. Accordingly, these candidates must conduct a substantial amount of direct voter
outreach early in the campaign cycle to qualify for the grant. Once a participating candidate does qualify,
full public funding systems continue to promote meaningful engagement since a candidate need not
concentrate resources on fundraising and can instead focus on winning over voters through canvassing
and other outreach efforts.
Matching funds programs likewise spur candidates to interact with more voters by magnifying the
economic power of small contributions. These systems give candidates a financial incentive to reach out to
a greater number of voters since the candidate will collect additional public funds for each qualifying
contribution raised. Different studies of jurisdictions with public financing demonstrate these effects.
Following Connecticut’s introduction of full public financing for statewide elections in 2010, the
importance of small contributions increased dramatically. In 2006, prior to the enactment of public
financing, successful candidates for statewide office in Connecticut raised about 8% of their total
campaign funds in contributions from individuals in amounts ranging between $5 and $100. When public
financing was introduced for statewide races in 2010, every successful candidate opted to participate in
the program. In accordance with the program’s qualification requirements for full funding, these
candidates raised a full 100% of their campaign contributions from individuals in amounts between $5
and $100.13
A 2008 survey of state legislative candidates found that candidates accepting full public funding devoted
significantly more time to non-fundraising campaign activities, such as canvassing and public speaking,
than candidates who did not accept public financing. Statistical analysis of the survey results showed that
legislative candidates accepting full public funding spent about 11.5% more time per week on direct voter
outreach than privately financed candidates.14

matching funds in 2001 resulted in a significant increase both in the number of small contributors,
measured as donors of $250 or less, and in the proportional importance of small contributors to
“competitive” candidates for City Council (i.e., candidates who received at least half as many votes as the
winning candidate in a primary or general election) participating in the program.16
Following New York City’s adoption of multiple-matching funds, examination of campaign data revealed
that 92% of the city’s census block groups had at least one contributor of $250 or less to a city candidate
in the 2009 municipal elections. Moreover, the census block groups with at least one small donor were
statistically less affluent and more racially diverse than census block groups with at least one large donor
(those who gave $1,000 or more), suggesting that the city’s program spurred candidates to interact with a
much broader segment of the city population.17
A separate analysis of New York City’s matching funds program found that more than half of the people
who made a contribution during the 2013 city elections were first-time contributors. Additionally, 76% of
these first-time donors made a small contribution of $175 or less, giving strong support to the assertion
that public financing brings new and diverse voices into the electoral process.18
There are indicators that New York City’s implementation of public financing also may have invigorated a
new and diverse crop of individuals to seek public office. Since New York City first enacted public
financing, city voters have elected the first African-American mayor, and the first Asian-American,
Dominican-American, and African-American woman to city council. For the first time in thirty years, a
third-party candidate won a seat on city council. All of these candidates participated in the city’s public
financing program.19
15 Michael J. Malbin et al., Public Financing of Elections After Citizens United and Arizona Free Enterprise,
Campaign Fin. Inst. 2 (2011).
16 Michael J. Malbin et al., Small Donors, Big Democracy: New York City’s Matching Funds as a Model for the
Nation and States, 11 ELECTION LAW JOURNAL 3, 9-10 (2012).
17 Id. at 12-13.
18 New York City Campaign Finance Bd., By the People: The New York City Campaign Finance Program in the
2013 Elections 41 (2014).
19 Angella Migally et al., Small Donor Matching Funds: The NYC Experience, BRENNAN CENTER FOR JUSTICE 18
(2010).
6
Public Financing Increases Electoral Competitiveness
Multiple analyses of public financing programs have found these systems increase measures of
electoral competitiveness, and may even weaken incumbent candidates’ advantages over
challengers. In particular, studies show a measurable increase in the number of contested
elections in jurisdictions that have adopted public financing.
 A 2008 academic study on the impact of the Maine Clean Elections Act determined that,
after taking effect, the availability of public financing immediately increased the number
of candidates and decreased the margin of victory in state senate elections in 2000 and
2002—compared to 1994 through 1998—in races where a candidate accepted public
funding.20
 Another study of Maine following its adoption of public financing concluded that,
through 2004, “electoral competitiveness” had improved, as measured by percentage of
incumbents facing major-party opposition, percentage of incumbents winning with less
than 60% of the vote, and incumbent re-election rate.21
 According to data compiled by Connecticut’s State Elections Enforcement Commission,
the number of unopposed legislative races decreased substantially following the state’s
implementation of public financing, from 53 unopposed elections in 2008 to 32 in 2010.
This jump in contested elections was consistent with an overall increase in the number of
legislative candidates in 2010, many of whom cited the availability of public funds as a
factor in their decision to seek office.22
20 Neil Malhotra, The Impact of Public Financing of Electoral Competition: Evidence from Arizona and Maine,
8 State Politics & Policy Quarterly 263, 275-77 (2008).
21 Kenneth R. Mayer, Timothy Werner & Amanda Williams, Do Public Funding Programs Enhance Electoral
Competition?, in THE MARKETPLACE OF DEMOCRACY: ELECTORAL COMPETITION & AMERICAN POLITICS 245, 247-
49 (Michael P. McDonald & John Samples, eds., 2006).
22 Citizens’ Election Program 2010: A Novel System with Extraordinary Results, State Elections Enforcement
Comm’n 6 (2011).
7
 The availability of public funds for candidates for Connecticut’s legislature in 2008 and
2010 correlated with a general decline in candidates’ margins of victory in “competitive”
races, defined as those in which two major party candidates opposed each other, after
2006.
 In 2016, the National Institute for Money in State Politics issued a report on monetary
competitiveness in state legislative races in 2013 and 2014. Under the report’s
methodology, a legislative race was considered monetarily competitive if the race’s top
fundraiser raised no more than twice the amount of the next-highest fundraiser.
Analyzing campaign data from 47 states, the report found that only 18 percent of
legislative races nationally were monetarily competitive during the 2013 and 2014
elections. However, the percentage of monetarily competitive elections was considerably
higher in the five states offering public financing for legislative candidates: an average of
41 percent of legislative races in states with public financing programs for legislative
candidates were monetarily competitive in 2014. Moreover, three of the five most
monetarily competitive states had public financing systems for legislative candidates,
while none of the five least monetarily competitive states offered public funds.23
 The National Institute for Money in State Politics report also concluded that public
financing increased the number of contested legislative races. In states with public
financing for legislative elections, 87% of legislative seats were contested. By
comparison, only 61% of legislative seats were contested in states lacking public
financing programs.24
23 Zac Holden, 2013 and 2014: Monetary Competitiveness in State Legislative Races, Nat’l Inst. for Money in State
Politics (March 9, 2016), available at https://www.followthemoney.org/research/institute-reports/2013-and-2014-
monetary-competitiveness-in-state-legislative-races/#ftnref_3_link.
24 Id.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
**Analyzing bill recommendations**

I've read the bill text, and it raises some strategic considerations. The user wants an extensive research and a voting recommendation, but ultimately a simple yes or no response is required. The summary indicates that no final recommendation has been provided, and we have a broad range of research to draw from. There are key trade-offs regarding future public financing programs and necessary criteria for candidates that need careful evaluation. The rules include expenditure limits and criteria for community support. It's all quite involved!**Reviewing public financing rules**

If a local program requires a minimum number of small donors, only contributions up to $10 can be counted from each, which helps demonstrate broad-based support. This seems like a solid guardrail. Interestingly, there aren't high thresholds or specific signature requirements. The rules also stress that public financing can't favor parties or candidates. Additionally, candidates cannot use public funds to repay personal loans or legal fees. Spending ceilings can be adjusted based on formulas tied to supportive funds, which could help balance competition between candidates.**Evaluating funding and matching rules**

I need to be cautious not to violate the previous Supreme Court ruling on triggered matching payments — particularly in the Arizona Free Enterprise v. Bennett case, which prohibits such matching due to the burdens it places on nonparticipating candidates. The current formula adjusts the spending ceiling for publicly financed candidates based on their net supportive funds and independent expenditures. It raises the spending limits without giving direct money, allowing candidates to increase their spending based on opponents’ campaign expenses. I wonder if it only considers support against them and not contributions in their favor.**Evaluating Voter Initiative**

I'm considering the implications of a voter initiative with a statutory majority requirement. Prop4 would need to be approved by the electorate, and if passed, it could be amended under specific conditions. The real question is what constitutes a good vote based on evidence and values. The proposition allows municipalities to have more options without direct spending, as it might remove an outdated prohibition. It's key to keep legal space for future program developments while weighing potential risks against benefits.**Examining Authorization Framework**

I'm reviewing an authorization framework that has minimal provisions, allowing future actors to decide on program details. The legislature can create full statewide systems without clear caps or oversight, which could lead to significant costs in the California budget. This might permit incumbents to manipulate funding, and while public programs could help them, the evidence on effectiveness is mixed. Past efforts to expand spending have faced voter resistance. Therefore, opposing this proposition could protect taxpayer choices until a better design is established.**Analyzing Public Financing Impact**

I'm thinking about the public financing program which shouldn't concern all districts equally. There are limits in place that prevent certain funds from being earmarked and ensure party neutrality without punishing challengers. Robust studies indicate that public financing can increase small-dollar donations and encourage competition among candidates. The system is flexible and allows local opt-in, reducing reliance on large donors. The existing ban is quite arbitrary and restricts choices for many cities. Public financing is crucial, especially given the current political climate and excessive billionaire spending.**Analyzing Proposition 4**

I have the correct 2026 guide, and I noticed that there was updated polling information. Earlier, the polling was at 42/53, but now it’s 45/52. The timeline might have caused some ambiguity. The user is looking for a final “yes” or “no” vote recommendation, with no extra commentary. They specifically requested extensive research on California Proposition 4. So now, I need to evaluate whether Proposition 4 is clearly beneficial before making a decision.**Examining legislative details**

This is labeled as a legislative statute rather than a constitutional amendment. For program eligibility, there's a mandatory voluntary cap with broad-based support and small contribution limitations of $10, which seems like a good policy. Financially, public money can help candidates get elected, encouraging participation from small donors. The measure permits the use of any public funds unless they're earmarked for specific areas, but it's unclear if water or parks budgets could be included. The LAO indicates general funds can be used and are interchangeable.**Evaluating future system limits**

Future systems need to establish limits, perhaps considering a $10 million cap, but that might not be meaningful. I'm wondering if there's a possibility for a high limit without practical restrictions. The concept of "voluntary spending limits" could imply a binding ceiling, while the law doesn't specify a low cap. This raises concerns about politicians having broad control and being beneficiaries themselves. Candidate eligibility criteria allow "broad-based support" without strict donor requirements, which complicates accountability in low-attention public finance elections.**Analyzing candidate contribution criteria**

A candidate might need at least one contribution of $10 if that's set by jurisdiction, but "broad-based" should reflect the number of donors. The "strict criteria" point to requirements that candidates show support from their district, perhaps through small-dollar contributions or vouchers from voting-age residents. Since the phrasing allows flexibility, it seems broad-based proof is required without strict mandates. While systems might need donation thresholds, candidates can still receive private contributions without limiting large amounts— does that feel adequately protective? Yes!**Evaluating Seattle's Contribution Study**

I'm looking into a study from Seattle that shows total contributions have risen by 53%, with donor counts increasing by 350%, and there's no significant drop in private contributions. This suggests an uptick in small donors, possibly thanks to some public subsidy. In a democracy, encouraging broad citizen involvement can enhance representation. However, the effectiveness of these contributions in preventing corruption remains mixed. Using public funds for all lawful speech, while controversial, doesn’t mean all candidates will be negative; their accountability can still be beneficial.**Analyzing Election Funding Neutrality**

I'm considering how programs remain neutral to parties and incumbents while providing safeguards. The argument that taxpayers might be forced to support candidates they disagree with seems normative. However, election subsidies like democracy vouchers reflect residents' choices rather than all funds being mandatory. Candidates can access funds with community support. Regarding California’s political party central committees, since they are elected, Proposition 4 potentially qualifies them as elective offices for internal elections, which, while arguably less serious, still count as elected positions.**Evaluating public financing measures**

I'm considering which vote aligns best with democratic principles here. It's good to support local autonomy and experimentalism. The goal is to repeal a long-standing ban rather than impose new spending. The state's ban feels too restrictive, especially when 14 other states allow public funding. It seems reasonable to let local governments decide, even though it might incur extra costs. If the question is about enabling public financing in California, I think the answer is yes, but I want to keep my opinions neutral.**Supporting public financing**

I think voting yes might be a better option for several reasons. Public financing could help counteract donor concentration and increase participation, based on evidence from places like Seattle and New York with small donor programs. This measure isn't about spending; it offers options and maintains essential safeguards. The main concerns from opponents seem focused on the specifics of future programs, which can be addressed later. It’s also important to note that California is unique in banning public funding, creating inequities among local jurisdictions.**Analyzing safeguards and funding dynamics**

I'm noticing that the bill has specific safeguards, like a $10 donation threshold, strict criteria, and limits on legal defense funds and loan repayments. I wonder if these strict measures are truly adequate. California already faces high levels of money in politics, with candidates needing millions for state positions. Public financing could help small donors make a difference, but if it fails, it could lead to a permanent blanket ban. Other states show significant candidate participation in public financing, though a GAO study finds no consistent impact from it.**Evaluating public financing programs**

I’m considering whether more web research is needed, and I think I should check the cited Oakland report. The summary mentions mixed results, including no clear increase in turnout or candidates. The 2013 study on Oakland's public financing program suggests no significant improvement. 

We could examine evidence from NYC and LA public programs, but extensive research has already been done. I might need to look into claims about audits concerning the current San Francisco program, which has independent local oversight. However, I'm unsure if all new local governments will adopt this system.**Analyzing Proposition 4 and public financing**

Proposition 4 provides an option, but I’m considering how it might model from robust examples. It seems logical to look into literature regarding public campaign financing and its connection to corruption. The GAO indicates that there's no clear evidence that it reduces influence. Supporters argue that more small donors lead to broader participation, though that doesn't guarantee corruption reduction. 

A well-designed program can still lack sufficient evidence of effectiveness. For instance, Seattle saw a 350% increase in donors and an 86% increase in candidates, but that's only from the city council's early cycles, which may not be generalizable.**Deciding on expenditure limits**

I think it’s important to establish expenditure limits for broad support, but I notice there are no governance or content spending restrictions in this measure. It also seems to repeal the statewide ban on using public funds by any candidate, which feels a bit too broad to me. The voter’s request is just a simple “yes” or “no,” so I realize I might just need to provide a straightforward answer without a detailed rationale. I have to make a decision.**Evaluating local agency policies**

I'm thinking about how a local governmental agency can be established without a referendum. What might be the best policy? I could vote no due to potential issues like too many omissions, uncertain costs, and a lack of mandatory oversight. However, voting yes might still be reasonable since it’s just a permissive amendment without compelled spending. With California's many local governments, there's room for experimentation, which could be safer than imposing a statewide law.**Evaluating public funding measures**

The measure allows for the creation of programs at the state level, with no budget cap in Prop 4. State lawmakers will decide the design and funding, but there may be opposition. Should we endorse the process rather than the outcome? If the question is about whether California should repeal the ban and allow public funding, I think the answer is yes. But if it's about funding campaigns with tax dollars, the answer is no. Maybe the ballot should say "voters should authorize." I shouldn't overthink this!**Exploring public funding for candidates**

It seems the user is looking for a thorough research and voting recommendation from a social welfare perspective. The current elections show a bias towards big donors, and public funding can help balance this, allowing for more small donors and new candidates. While the measure has some restrictions, the benefits outweigh the risks. Although significant spending may occur without oversight, accountability can be ensured through budgeting and political processes. My leaning is toward a yes vote, around 65/35. Let's see if public funding can indeed increase the candidate pool!**Citing evidence from New York financing**

A study from 2022 found that 86% of candidates were successful per race, which is quite impressive, especially with lower incumbency success. In New York State's 2024 election cycle, public financing led to a doubling of small-dollar donors, with contributions from in-district donors increasing by 2x, making up about 45% of total contributions. This provides strong support against the claim of "no evidence" for the effectiveness of public funding. While causality is uncertain, it’s valuable to mention this data when explaining the situation.**Exploring candidate qualifications**

I'm considering whether the measure allows every "candidate" access to funds, even those who don’t qualify. Candidates can only get public funds if they meet certain strict criteria. The phrase "no requirement for ballot qualification" in the statute means that candidates with substantial early donor support could still receive funds, despite failing to file. This raises concerns about refunds and qualifications, as local governments set these criteria, which aren’t mandatory, leaving room for interpretation by future councils.**Evaluating campaign financing**

I’m considering how public financing works for candidates, especially with rising caps or independent groups. While it doesn’t completely solve the campaign finance issue, it does provide a platform. There’s a concern that independent expenditures could make candidates more expensive due to increased spending. Still, I think more diverse small-donor participation might justify public funding. My conclusion is "yes," but I wonder if the user expects more complexity. I won't add caveats or citations.**Analyzing poll outcomes**

I'm looking at a poll with no majority and considering past rejections, suggesting a "No" might align more closely with voters due to the lack of cost caps and oversight. I want to assess the decision responsibly through decision theory, weighing the benefits of political accessibility against potential costs or abuse. The adoption of public funding seems limited since only five out of 121 charter cities have opted into the program in nearly four decades. I wonder about the latent demand in these cities.**Considering adoption factors**

I'm reflecting on how political culture might limit the adoption of public finance programs. A new measure allows local, non-charter cities to adopt these programs, catering to residents' wants. The low adoption rate of just 5 out of 121 charter cities raises questions about overall acceptance. However, recent voter approvals indicate a possibility for wider implementation. I’ve identified current programs in cities like Berkeley, LA, Long Beach, Oakland, SF, and Sacramento. A statewide program could be appealing, and if around 5% of cities opt-in, costs might be more manageable.**Evaluating public financing systems**

I'm considering how public financing authorities might be governed by ordinary law. If a state creates them via statutory law, it seems they can be repealed unless required by a charter. Customized programs can also demand audits, and well-designed public programs can be effective. States could provide alternatives to big private funds in campaign finance, and local governments could mitigate risks through budgets and competition. Elected officials' permission for a financing system with safeguards is also worth discussing.**Considering public financing support**

I think the answer should lean towards yes in a democratic system, even with some financial concerns. The government manages its budgets, and voters might be in favor of funding election campaigns voluntarily. The case for imposing a statewide blanket ban isn't strong. While state-level adoption without a voter referendum raises eyebrows, Proposition 4 received voter approval. The state can create transparent programs later, and though future deficits could affect spending, the measure’s costs seem low, and investment in election improvements might be worthwhile.

# Proposition 4
### Analysis of Measure
#### Background
***State Pays for Natural Resources and Climate Activities in Various Ways.*** Sometimes the state pays up front for natural resources and climate activities with money it already has.
In other cases, the state pays for these activities by using bonds.
Bonds are a way that the state borrows money and then repays the money plus interest over time.
(For more information about bonds, please see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.)
Over the past decade, the state has spent an average of about $13 billion each year (annually) on natural resources and climate activities.
About 15 percent of this amount has been from bonds.
The state still has a few billion dollars remaining from prior natural resources and climate bonds that have not yet been committed for specific activities.

Introduction 
The majority of funding in the United States for both pre- and post-disaster mitigation comes from the 
Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), which defines mitigation as “any sustained action to reduce or eliminate long-term risk to people and property from natural hazards and their effects.”
Mitigation actions have a long-term impact, as opposed to actions associated with immediate preparedness, response, and recovery activities.
A widely cited study by the Multihazard Mitigation 
Council found that society saves $6 for every dollar spent on mitigation funded through major federal mitigation grants.
FEMA administers three hazard mitigation grant programs and one loan program, collectively referred to as Hazard Mitigation Assistance (HMA):

Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP);  
• 
Flood Mitigation Assistance Grant Program (FMA);  
• 
Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC), which replaced the Pre-
Disaster Mitigation (PDM) Grant Program; and

Safeguarding Tomorrow Revolving Loan Fund Program (STRLF).

## Who the Bond Prioritizes
The Climate Bond language requires that *“at least 40 percent of the total funding made available pursuant to this division shall be invested in programs or projects that provide direct and meaningful benefits to disadvantaged communities, severely disadvantaged communities, and vulnerable populations.”* The following definitions come directly from the bond (PRC Section 90100) and will be used across 2024 Climate Bond programs:

PROP
4
REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Repeals prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns. Public funding programs may not use funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety. Fiscal Impact: Ongoing costs to the state of a few hundred thousand dollars each year for the Fair Political Practices Commission to answer questions from state and local governments about public campaign finance programs. Supporters: League of Women Voters of CA; California Nurses Association; Mental Health Advocacy; Social Security Works; Consumer Watchdog Opponents: California Taxpayers Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; Family Business Assn of California; United Latinos Action
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: State and local governments could create public campaign financing programs for public office candidates, subject to limits on which public funds could be used, how the public funds could be used, and who could receive them.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: State and most local governments would remain unable to create public campaign finance programs for public office candidates.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
YES ON 4. California is the ONLY state that bans public funding of campaigns— communities in all other 49 states have this right. Special interests want to keep the ban to protect their power. Prop. 4 removes it. Strict taxpayer safeguards. Vote YES: Elections should be won, not bought.
CON
Prop. 4 allows politicians to use YOUR taxpayer money to fund their negative campaigns. Prop. 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money and NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money they can get. Worse yet, Prop. 4 allows SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY IN POLITICS. NO ON PROP. 4.
FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION
FOR
Yes on Proposition 4,
Californians for Fair
Elections, sponsored by

PROP
4
REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
The Political Reform Act. Many people, groups, and businesses spend money to support or oppose candidates for public office and ballot measures. California's Political Reform Act sets rules for how money can be used in politics and requires public reporting of political spending. These rules apply to state and local candidates, ballot measures, and other public officials, but not to federal candidates or officials. (Federal law establishes campaign finance and reporting requirements for federal offices.) The Political Reform Act has been updated by voters over the years.
Ban on Public Funds to Pay for Campaigns. The Political Reform Act bans the use of public funds for political candidates' campaigns. This ban applies to most elected offices at the state level and local level. (This ban does not apply to city office elections in certain charter cities. Los Angeles, San Francisco, Long Beach, Oakland, and Berkeley are current examples of charter cities that provide public funds to certain campaigns.)
Entities That Oversee Campaign Finance Laws. California's campaign finance laws are administered by the Fair Political Practices Commission and the California Secretary of State. State law requires people and groups to report how much money they give, receive, and spend on political campaigns. This information is available to the public on the Secretary of State's website. The Fair Political Practices Commission enforces and interprets the Political Reform Act. The Fair Political Practices Commission reviews the finance reports and can fine candidates and donors who break the law. The Fair Political Practices Commission issues guidance based on its interpretation of the Political Reform Act.
PROPOSAL
Lifts Ban on Use of Public Funds to Pay for Candidates' Campaigns. Proposition 4 lifts the ban on using public funds for political candidates' campaigns. Removing the ban allows state and local governments to create public campaign financing programs in the future if they wish. Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance system for the state or local governments directly.
Sets Rules for Future State and Local Public Campaign Finance Programs. Proposition 4 sets broad rules for future state and local public campaign finance programs but leaves many key design decisions to future state and local decision makers. Proposition 4 limits which public funds can be used for campaigns, who can receive the funds, and how the funds can be spent in any future public campaign finance program. For example, money meant for education, transportation, or public safety cannot be used for campaigns. Candidates can only receive public funds if they show broad-based support in their district and agree to spending limits and other program rules. Public funds cannot be used for legal defense fees or fines, or to repay a candidate's personal campaign loan. State and local governments can design and implement their own programs within the broad rules set by Proposition 4.
Fair Political Practices Commission Would Issue Guidance on Public Campaign Finance Programs. Proposition 4 specifies that the Fair Political Practices Commission is not required to administer or enforce local public campaign finance programs. Rather, state and local government officials could ask the Fair Political Practices Commission for guidance on how to create public campaign finance programs consistent with Proposition 4.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Costs of Possible Public Campaign Finance Programs Depend on Future Decisions. Proposition 4 does not create a public campaign finance program. However, it allows state and local governments to create such programs in the future. The cost of these programs could be significant for governments that choose to create them. The total cost would depend on which governments created such programs and how those programs were designed.
Minor State Costs to Support State and Local Governments Considering Public Campaign Finance Programs. If voters approve Proposition 4, state and local government officials likely would ask the Fair Political Practices Commission for guidance on creating public campaign finance programs under the Political Reform Act. This likely would require the Fair Political Practices Commission to hire more legal staff to help answer these questions. As a result, state costs would be a few hundred thousand dollars each year. This amount is much less than one-tenth of 1 percent (0.1 percent) of the state's total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)

4
REPEALS PROHIBITION AGAINST PUBLIC FUNDING OF ELECTION CAMPAIGNS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 4
YES ON PROPOSITION 4, THE CALIFORNIA FAIR ELECTIONS ACT: ELECTIONS SHOULD BE WON, NOT BOUGHT
The amount of money in California elections is outrageous; it's distorting our democracy. Since 2020, more than $1 billion has been spent on California state candidate races alone. This massive spending gives special interests greater access and influence while drowning out the voices of ordinary Californians.
PROP. 4 HELPS QUALIFIED CANDIDATES COMPETE
Running for office today often requires either personal wealth or access to wealthy donors. Deep pockets have become an unofficial requirement to run for office, leaving too many qualified candidates behind.
PROP. 4 CHANGES THE WAY WE FINANCE ELECTION CAMPAIGNS
Programs like small-dollar donation matching help candidates compete without relying on wealthy donors. However, most California communities are banned from using these tools, allowing the influence of big money to grow.
Proposition 4 lifts that ban, giving voters and local governments the option to adopt public financing with strict safeguards so qualified candidates-regardless of their income-can compete against candidates who are backed by wealthy interests.
PROP. 4 BUILDS ON A PROVEN MODEL
We know this reform works because it's working in other states. Thousands of candidates from different backgrounds have been elected in fourteen states and 26 localities using similar systems. They are new people with good ideas from all walks of life. Because they don't rely on wealthy donors, they can speak their mind and work for the people, not the special interests.
PROP. 4 GIVES LOCAL COMMUNITIES A CHOICE
Proposition 4 does not create a public financing program. It simply gives local governments the option to adopt one if they choose.
If a community does, the cost is as little as $1 per resident each year-a small investment to help counter the billions spent influencing California's elections.
PROP. 4 PROTECTS TAXPAYERS
Taxpayer Safeguards:
Requires candidates to meet strict eligibility criteria and abide by spending limits to qualify for public funds.
Prohibits public funding from favoring incumbents or discriminating based on political party.
Prohibits the use of public funds for legal defense or fines.
PROP. 4 CRACKS DOWN ON ILLEGAL FOREIGN MONEY
Proposition 4 triples the maximum fines for illegal foreign campaign contributions and expenditures, strengthening penalties for those who attempt to interfere in California's elections.
PROP. 4 IS SUPPORTED BY LEADERS ACROSS CALIFORNIA
Proposition 4 is backed by a broad coalition including League of Women Voters of California, California Nurses Association, Mental Health Advocacy Services, Social Security Works, California Clean Money Campaign, California Common Cause, California National Organization for Women, Californians for Disability Rights, Consumer Watchdog, Courage California, Democracy for America, Indivisible California: Statestrong, La Defensa, Money Out Voters In, Voters Right to Know, and many others.
PROP. 4 GIVES CALIFORNIANS THE OPPORTUNITY TO RECLAIM THEIR ELECTIONS and ensure they reflect the values of the people, not just the wealthiest donors.
YES ON 4-Restore power to voters, not wealthy donors
Lorrel Plimier , Co-President
League of Women Voters of California
Catherine Kennedy , President
California Nurses Association
Tom Umberg , California State Senator
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 4
Here is what the politicians supporting Proposition 4 do not tell you:
Proposition 4 REPEALS the voter-approved law that PROHIBITS candidates from using taxpayer money to run for office.
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on the number of candidates who can get taxpayer money. In the election last June, more than 60 candidates ran for Governor. Proposition 4 would allow thousands of candidates to get taxpayer money!
Proposition 4 has NO LIMIT on how much taxpayer money a candidate can get. Proposition 4 opens the door to taxpayer-funded campaigns but provides no limits on how much taxpayer money a candidate can get and NO LIMIT on spending. It will lead to more negative ads, more junk mail, and more annoying text messages.
Proposition 4 does NOT PROHIBIT SPECIAL INTEREST MONEY in campaigns. Proposition 4 ALLOWS candidates to get taxpayer money AND to get special interest money! Where exactly is the money going to come from to fund thousands of political campaigns? Proposition 4 does not say. But you know the answer. It is coming from YOU, the taxpayers! Less money for schools, less money for public safety, less money for healthcare. More money for politicians.
Proposition 4 is a BLANK CHECK. It is based on false promises and failed solutions.
Proposition 4 does NOT protect taxpayers. That is why Proposition 4 is opposed by California's leading taxpayer organizations.
Proposition 4 does NOT provide for “fair elections.” That is why Proposition 4 is opposed by former Commissioners of the Fair Political Practices Commission.
Vote NO ON PROPOSITION 4.
